title: Census Data Analysis
summary: A team research paper on how education, age, sex, and race relate to salary.
tagline: A research paper for UNC Charlotte's Data and Society course that examines race, sex, years of education, and age as predictors of earning more than $50,000, using a subset of 1996 U.S. Census data.
role: Co-authored the paper as part of a five-person team: data preparation, statistical analysis, visualization, and writing.
team: Davis Higgins, Chris Loor-Luna, Cory Nguyen, Tam Khong, and Jeffrey Alvarez (DTSC 1302, December 2024).
problem: Income disparities are easy to describe and hard to interpret. The research question was which predictor, or combination of predictors, has the most significant impact on salary: race, sex, years of education, or age.
contribution: This was a five-person team paper. I co-authored it with Chris Loor-Luna, Cory Nguyen, Tam Khong, and Jeffrey Alvarez, contributing to the data preparation, analysis, visualizations, and written findings.
solution: The team defined salary as a binary outcome (above or at most $50,000), one-hot encoded race categories, and treated years of education and age as continuous predictors. We used chi-square tests for categorical relationships, one-way ANOVA to compare means across groups, and Pearson correlation for continuous variables, supported by three visualizations.

architecture.summary: Variables were defined first, then each relationship was tested with the method that fits its data type.

decisions.title: Match the test to the variable.
decisions.text: Categorical pairs used chi-square, group mean comparisons used ANOVA, and continuous pairs used Pearson correlation.

decisions.title: Distinguish correlation from causation.
decisions.text: The paper reports which predictors are most strongly associated with income without claiming they cause it.

decisions.title: Keep the artifact available.
decisions.text: The full paper is published beside the case study so every claim can be checked.

outcomes: Years of education showed the strongest positive relationship with earning more than $50,000, followed by age, consistent with the hypothesis that education is a key determinant of earning potential. Sex and race showed weaker relationships, with disparities between categories.
limits: The data is a 1996 Census subset with a binary income threshold, so the results describe associations in that sample rather than current wages or causal effects. The paper notes non-response bias and the binary classification as limitations.
lessons: A clear statistical argument depends on explaining variables and uncertainty, not just ranking predictors.
